T21.problem: A national truckers' strike (9–12 Nov), joined by intercity buses and No+TAG, blocked highways over diesel prices after six consecutive rises. On 15 Nov, 97% had heard of it and about 80% backed it (Cadem, Criteria); 86% found it justified.
T21.politics: The government withdrew its $20 cap bill on 11 Nov and agreed with two truckers' confederations on 12 Nov: diesel −$142 per litre, wider tax and toll refunds, and rises frozen until 7 Apr 2027 in the bill (the 12 Nov deal said 31 Mar) (cost put at US$500m by Hacienda on 12 Nov, about US$700m on 16 Nov, and up to US$1bn by others). Independents and No+TAG stayed mobilised. The bill, under 'discusión inmediata', passed the Chamber Finance committee unanimously on 16 Nov; 66% back the measures.

newTopics.name: Economic slowdown and technical recession
newTopics.problem: The Central Bank expectations survey cut 2026 growth to 0% (10 Nov). The Finance Minister said the economy is 'technically' in recession after two quarterly contractions (11 Nov). Q3 GDP on 18 Nov.
newTopics.politics: No growth plan or bill. 60% expect the economy to worsen (Criteria, 15 Nov). The government's line is fiscal consolidation.

newTopics.name: Child protection: waiting lists and Mejor Niñez funding
newTopics.problem: The Children's Ombudsman's annual report: more than 41,000 children waiting for protection places, and cuts in 102 of 197 budget items (CIPER, 12 Nov).

newTopics.name: Science ministry: internal crisis and the science budget
newTopics.timing: President's decision on the ministry pending; Senate budget vote 17–19 Nov
newTopics.problem: The Science line of Budget 2027 was rejected in the mixed committee; the university rectors' council (CRUCh) puts the 2027 budget at a 10% real cut on 2026, putting Fondequip, Fondef, FIU, InES and graduate scholarships at risk (El Mercurio, 2 Nov). The Academy of Sciences warns lost capacity could take decades to recover. Coverage this week is about the internal conflict, not the cuts.
newTopics.politics: An open conflict between Minister Lincolao and Undersecretary Rossi since late October (a Ley Karin complaint, adviser exits, dismissals on 13 Nov without the undersecretary's knowledge). La Moneda sent staff, Interior Minister Alvarado intervened (16 Nov) and the spokesperson said the ministry 'has not worked as we expected' (17 Nov). Hacienda rejected the minister's tax incentive in the AI bill.
newTopics.frames: Mismanagement and a divided team (government and press) vs. a budget cut that harms science (scientific community, CRUCh). Not converging.
newTopics.changed: New topic, from the reviewer's lead. A change of people (Kingdon) can open a window: a new minister often brings a new agenda, here possibly a restored science budget or a different AI policy.

New topic. Level 1: the science budget cut is real but drew little attention this week; the conflict, not the cut, is the story. Would rise to 2 if the scientific community or the Senate debate makes the cut visible.

New topic. Level 2: the government has openly acknowledged the problem and the President's decision is pending, a formal step short of a decision. If the minister or undersecretary is replaced, a new team can bring a new agenda (Kingdon: change of people), so this is the place to watch for a window, especially if the science budget is restored in the Senate.

stories.title: Approval falls to the lowest of the term
stories.text: Criteria put approval at 18% (−6) and Cadem at 27% (−2) on 15 Nov, after the fuel rise and the truckers' strike. About 80% backed the strike, and 60% expect the economy to worsen.

stories.title: The truckers' deal sets up a fuel law
stories.text: The strike ended on 12 Nov with a $142 diesel cut and a price freeze that the bill extends to 7 April, at a cost of US$500m to US$1bn depending on who counts. The bill passed the Chamber Finance committee unanimously on 16 Nov, so the window is likely to close this week with a decision.

stories.title: The Chamber rejects seven budget lines
stories.text: Budget 2027 reached the Senate with seven ministry lines rejected (six on the Chamber floor, Science earlier in committee) and without its US$25bn borrowing authorisation. Under the new budget rule this counts as a problem event; the Senate votes 17–19 Nov.

conceptSignals.rationale: Why a focusing event: the truckers' strike of 9–12 Nov was sudden and visible (highways blocked in several regions, buses and No+TAG joining) and put fuel prices in front of the whole country at once. It happened in W9; it is listed here because the deal, the bill and the polls of this week all follow from it. No new event since 13 Nov.

review.note: Yes, but just consider somewhere that the agreement with the govenrment might have closed the window

conceptSignals.rationale: Why salience: 97% had heard of the truckers' strike (Criteria, 15 Nov), which measures attention. Strength 2, one poll. The figures on agreement with the strikers (about 80%) are mood, not attention, and are counted once, under politics.

Why frame consensus: actors on different sides now describe the March price pass-through as the mistake. This week that rests on one voice (the PDG leader); in W9 a centre-right senator said the same. Weak until more sides repeat it.
Why feedback: the first information on how the response performs. Cost estimates rose from about US$500m to US$700–900m and an economist warns of reallocations in 2027. One source.

Why government intention: the executive signed a deal with two truckers' confederations (12 Nov) and three ministers or undersecretaries defended it in public this week. A written, costed commitment is the strongest form of intention.
Why an agenda tool: the bill entered Congress with 'discusión inmediata', the strongest urgency, which forces both chambers to vote within days.

Why coalition or vote: the Chamber Finance committee approved the bill unanimously on 16 Nov, UDI backs it and both chambers coordinated to pass it by 17 Nov. Strength 2 rather than 3 because the floor votes had not happened by 16 Nov.

Why national mood: about 80% backed the strike (Cadem 79%, Criteria 80%) and 66% back the diesel cut and the freeze (Cadem). Two pollsters; the three items report the same two polls. The mood supports the move, so nothing is deducted from the politics level. This is the fact the reviewer called the most critical in W9.

Why organised forces: two confederations accepted the deal and ended the strike, but independents in La Araucanía and Antofagasta and No+TAG stayed mobilised, and the largest confederation says the government acted late. Pressure is easing, not gone.

Why salience: 79% disagree with keeping Minister Rabat (+7 points; 64% even on the right) and 72% back his removal (Criteria, 15 Nov), after Cadem made the reductions the top reason for disapproval in W9. One poll this week, reported by two outlets. The second check notes that 'disagree with keeping the minister' is closer to mood than to attention; the reviewer may prefer to count it under politics.

Why frame consensus: Matthei, from the governing side's sector, called the handling of the case absurd, so criticism is no longer only from the opposition. One source this week. (UDI's president also called the decrees 'a serious political error', coded under politics.)

Why coalition or vote: the accusation was filed (12 Nov) and its review committee drawn with a 3–2 opposition majority (16 Nov), which is a formal step. But the opposition has about 65 of the 78 votes, the PDG swing bloc (14) will not commit, and UDI and the governing coalition expect to reject it. Strength 2: step taken, outcome open.

Why government intention: from Vietnam the President took responsibility and confirmed full support for Rabat. The executive intends to resist, not act; since executive signals take precedence, this holds the stream at 2.

Why indicator change: the Central Bank's job-ads index fell for a twelfth month (W9, one source). No new labour indicator this week; INE publishes on 27 Nov. The stream level of 2 is carried from the reviewed W9.
Why salience: one talk-show episode on unemployment as the top concern (W9). As the reviewer noted, coverage this week is thin.

Why national mood: 53% expect job prospects to worsen (Criteria, 15 Nov), in two outlets. Mood only: no government move on employment this week, so by the same rule used for Growth & recession the stream level is 1.

Why a focusing event: the Chamber sent the budget to the Senate with seven ministry lines (six on the Chamber floor in votes on 10–13 Nov: Education, Interior, Segegob, Mining, Women, Culture; Science had already lost its funds in the mixed committee) and without the authorisation to borrow up to US$25bn, which the press called a defeat for the government. Under the budget rule a rejection is the kind of event that makes the budget a problem. Caution from the second check: rejecting lines in the Chamber and restoring them in the Senate is a fairly common budget cycle, and there is no sign of public attention.

Why government intention: the Finance Minister promised to restore the rejected lines in the Senate and keeps the consolidation target while paying about US$700m for the truckers' deal. Three outlets. It is a promise: no funds have been restored yet, so it is not coded as use of the budget tool.
Why coalition or vote: the Chamber result shows the government lacks a majority for its budget as drafted. This arithmetic is the reason the stream is held at 2 instead of 3.

Why coalition or vote: the Chamber approved the Health budget 82–41, restored primary-care funds and raised Ricarte Soto funding. A decision in one chamber; the Senate remains. No problem-stream item this week.

Why a focusing event: the amendment to restore the Education budget failed 72–72 on 11 Nov, so Education stays rejected. One event (W9), reported by two outlets; the 16 Nov item is a recap, not a second rejection. A failed vote is an event under the budget rule. No measure of public attention yet.
Why organised forces: the teachers' union called a national march and work stoppage for 24 Nov over the education budget. One outlet, reporting the union's own call.
Why government intention: the truckers' deal doubles the toll refund for intercity buses, from 35% to 70% (W9 item coded under fuel prices). A commitment inside a signed deal.
Why organised forces: No+TAG joined the blockades demanding lower tolls, a flat tariff and forgiveness of TAG debts, and said it had no agreement with the government (W9).
Why national mood: 64% support the higher toll refund (Cadem). One poll question, one outlet.
Why indicator change: the Central Bank's expectations survey cut 2026 growth to 0% (10 Nov). A primary source; Q3 GDP on 18 Nov will confirm or ease it.

Why frame consensus: the Finance Minister himself said the economy is 'technically' in recession, adopting the critics' description. One actor, so strength 1; it becomes consensus if the opposition and business describe it the same way.

Why national mood: 60% expect the economy to worsen in six months (+11), Criteria 15 Nov, in two outlets (items coded under Employment). The stream stays at 1 because mood without a government step is 'public demand without action' on the level scale.
Why indicator change: the Children's Ombudsman reports more than 41,000 children waiting for protection places. One source (CIPER, citing Emol).
Why feedback: Matthei called the government's security plan 'pure bluff', a judgement on how an existing plan performs. One voice, no data.
Why coalition or vote: regional budget lines passed the Chamber without rejection, credited to the earlier agreement with governors. Confirms a decision already taken.

Why government approval: Criteria 18% (−6), Cadem 27% (−2), both the lowest of the term, reported by seven outlets, with Panel Ciudadano near 20%. A decisive change that narrows room for unpopular moves.

Why national mood: 84% said the government should have acted sooner on fuel prices. The public is against the government's handling but in favour of the measures now on the table. Same two polls as the fuel-prices mood check, so not counted as new evidence.
Why events within government: criticism of La Moneda's advisers from inside the coalition, the President abroad until 22 Nov, and no cabinet change. Mentions only.

Why government intention: Hacienda offered to restore education funds in the Senate and review the 'Yo elijo mi PC' programme (item coded under the Budget topic). One source, a promise, no amendment filed.

Why events within government: the minister and the undersecretary are in open conflict (dismissals on 13 Nov without the undersecretary's knowledge), the Interior Minister stepped in on 16 Nov and the spokesperson said on 17 Nov that the ministry 'has not worked as we expected' and the President 'will decide'. Four outlets; the spokesperson's statement is first-hand and decisive, because it puts a change of people on the table.

conceptSignals.rationale: Why government intention: the government dropped the minister's tax incentive from the AI bill after Hacienda objected, while the minister signs agreements with AI firms abroad. Two signals of what the executive intends on science and AI policy, pulling in different directions.

Why a focusing event: under the budget rule, the Science line rejected in the mixed committee and the 10% real cut reported by CRUCh are the kind of event that makes the budget a problem. Strength 1 for now: this week's coverage is about the conflict, not the cuts, and the evidence (El Mercurio, 2 Nov, citing CRUCh; and the mixed committee's rejection, coded under Budget) predates this week, so no item is cited here. The Friday run should code the Senate's decision on the line.
